dNaViT: Discrete Codes are General-Purpose Visual Representations

Abstract

Discrete autoregressive modeling, notably through next-token prediction, has become a cornerstone of modern language models. Extending this paradigm to vision allows visual and language models to converge on a unified framework, thereby fostering shared methodology and infrastructure. This work investigates a central question: how far can a finite discrete vocabulary go in representing the richness of the visual world? We present dNaViT, a Discrete Native-resolution Vision Transformer that produces discrete visual primitives analogous to language tokens. Built upon a frozen pretrained encoder, dNaViT applies lightweight residual modulation with a dual-branch objective to inject reconstruction-aware cues into semantic features. By leveraging grouped product quantization, it scales discrete capacity without inflating spatial sequence lengths, while a balanced training recipe maintains both semantic and pixel-level information. Consequently, dNaViT functions as a versatile discrete visual tokenizer, enabling unified encoding across downstream tasks alongside high-fidelity image decoding. Extensive evaluations show that dNaViT matches or exceeds task-specific baselines across 12 visual understanding benchmarks, 4 generation benchmarks, and an image editing benchmark. These findings demonstrate that a compact discrete vocabulary can serve as a universal visual currency and unlock the full potential of fully unified, native multimodal methodology.

1 Introduction

Language models have achieved remarkable success through next-token prediction, anchored by discrete tokens as their fundamental modeling unit (Brown et al., 2020). From the perspective of compression as intelligence (Delétang et al., 2023), discrete tokens provide a unified substrate for representation learning and autoregressive modeling. In contrast, modern multimodal models frequently rely on modality-specific representations and heterogeneous learning objectives (Caffagni et al., 2024). This paradigm divergence disconnects vision from the established techniques and scalable infrastructure to language, raising a foundational question: can visual information be represented losslessly like language using a learned discrete vocabulary?

Discrete visual representations offer a promising bridge, naturally aligning visual inputs with autoregressive language architectures under a unified token-prediction objective (Xie et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024b; Zou et al., 2026b; Peng et al., 2026; Meituan LongCat Team et al., 2026; Cui et al., 2025). However, discretizing dense, continuous visual signals into a finite vocabulary presents a severe information bottleneck (Ma et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2026) that hinders performance. Crucially, harmonizing high-level semantic abstraction for understanding with fine-grained pixel details for high-fidelity reconstruction within a single discrete bottleneck remains an unresolved tension (Wu et al., 2024; Qu et al., 2025).

To answer the question posed above and address these challenges, we introduce dNaViT, a Discrete Native-resolution Vision Transformer that extends our preliminary work in LongCat-Next (Meituan LongCat Team et al., 2026). Following the representation encoder paradigm (Zheng et al., 2025), dNaViT enriches the semantic features of a frozen pretrained encoder with pixel details through a Residual Modulator (ResMod), without compromising its underlying semantic capability. The resulting features are discretized into a shared vocabulary using Grouped Product Quantization (PQ) (Jégou et al., 2011) under dual-branch representation and pixel reconstruction loss. Training progresses through continuous initialization, discrete feature alignment, and final joint optimization, which balance theses objectives and suppress gradient interference.

These design choices yield a shared discrete interface for tasks that conventionally rely on separate visual encodings, extending the utility of pretrained representations beyond their original objectives. By rotating and translating pretrained features, residual modulation reorganizes their geometry to accommodate reconstruction-relevant information, making more effective use of the available representational capacity. Combined with sufficient factorized code capacity, this allows semantic structure and fine-grained detail to coexist within a shared discrete bottleneck, mitigating information loss during quantization. The resulting tokenizer brings the flexibility of text tokenization to vision: images can be encoded into discrete sequences and decoded into faithful reconstructions, while the codes retain semantic information closely aligned with language.

We evaluate the generality of dNaViT across four core capabilities: image reconstruction, classification, multimodal understanding, generation, editing. Driven by a single shared discrete vocabulary with a spatial downsampling factor f=32f=32, dNaViT achieves 28.12​ dB28.12\text{\penalty\ dB} PSNR and 0.810.81 SSIM at 512×512512\times 512 resolution without sacrificing semantic representation capability. When paired with Qwen3-8B, dNaViT surpasses prior discrete baselines and rivals Qwen3-VL-8B across key document and reasoning benchmarks, scoring 885885 on OCRBench. For image generation and editing, dNaViT achieve impressive performance on GenEval2 (49.549.5) and outperforms open-weight baselines on Qwen-Image-Bench (52.252.2), while excelling at bilingual text rendering. Crucially, dNaViT establishes these comprehensive understanding and generation capabilities under a substantially reduced data budget relative to existing models.

These findings suggest that the gap between continuous visual signals and discrete tokens is a challenge of representation learning rather than an inherent limitation. With appropriate modeling, discrete codes can serve as general-purpose visual primitives, bringing vision and language into a shared token-based paradigm. Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  1. 1.

    This work explores the question of whether discrete codes can serve as general-purpose visual primitives, analogous to the role of tokens in language modeling. To investigate this possibility, we introduce dNaViT, a native-resolution visual tokenizer designed to capture both high-level semantic structure and fine-grained pixel information within a shared vocabulary for different tasks.

  2. 2.

    dNaViT uses residual modulation to aggregate multi-level features from a frozen vision encoder and grouped product quantization to encode the enriched representations. Progressive training coordinates dual-branch semantic and pixel reconstruction objectives. Experiments demonstrate that this design balances semantic preservation and reconstruction fidelity within the discrete bottleneck.

  3. 3.

    Comprehensive evaluations across visual understanding, image reconstruction, generation, and editing demonstrate dNaViT’s generality. With a substantially smaller training data budget than the compared models, dNaViT achieves strong understanding and generation performance, highlighting the effectiveness and data efficiency of its unified, language-aligned representation.

  4. 4.

    This work demonstrates that a shared discrete token space can serve as a universal visual currency, providing a general-purpose intermediate representation across complementary tasks and a foundation for fully unified, native multimodal modeling.

2 dNaViT

This section presents dNaViT, a visual tokenizer that learns shared discrete codes as a unified interface for diverse downstream tasks, replacing separate task-specific feature representations. We will describe how the architecture supports these capabilities while mitigating conflicts between semantic abstraction and fine-grained detail preservation, as well as information loss during discretization.

2.1 Background

Visual modeling has largely relied on distinct continuous representations for different downstream tasks: pretrained semantic features for multimodal understanding (Tschannen et al., 2025) and reconstruction-oriented latents for diffusion-based synthesis (Rombach et al., 2022). Representation autoencoders bridge these approaches by pairing pretrained semantic encoders with reconstruction decoders (Zheng et al., 2025). By contrast, language models use discrete tokens as a uniform representation of text, supporting a unified, scalable next-token prediction framework. Meanwhile, recent benchmarks (An et al., 2026a; Yan et al., 2026) highlight the growing need to integrate linguistic and visual intelligence to solve real-world tasks.

Extending this framework to vision is challenging: unlike the discrete symbols of language, visual signals encode dense, continuous variation. Discrete visual tokenization addresses this by mapping images to sequences of codebook indices. For example, vector-quantized autoencoders assign continuous features to learned codebook entries and reconstruct images from the corresponding embeddings (van den Oord et al., 2017). These indices can be embedded and predicted like text tokens, enabling a shared autoregressive interface and the reuse of language-model architectures and objectives. Chameleon (Chameleon Team, 2024) and Emu3 (Wang et al., 2024b) demonstrate this formulation for multimodal understanding and generation. However, information loss during tokenization can constrain downstream performance and the benefits of scaling.

A shared token interface alone does not guarantee that the learned codes jointly preserve semantic information and fine-grained visual detail, both of which are essential to general-purpose visual modeling. Prior studies have examined the distinct information requirements of understanding and reconstruction (Qu et al., 2025) and identified limited discrete capacity as a key bottleneck in supporting both objectives (Ma et al., 2025). Motivated by these findings, dNaViT aims to preserve complementary task-relevant information within a shared discrete vocabulary and match the performance of task-specific representations.

2.2 Overall Architecture

Motivated by the exploration of information recovery through residual connections (Meituan LongCat Team et al., 2026), dNaViT further propose residual modulation to aggregate complementary cues and enrich the features of a frozen native-resolution vision encoder with reconstruction-relevant detail (Fig. 3). To preserve both semantic structure and visual detail within a shared discrete bottleneck, we quantize the enriched features using grouped product quantization and supervise the resulting codes through dual reconstruction branches. Progressive training coordinates these objectives to mitigate interference during optimization.

2.3 Representation Encoder

Unified visual tokenization must reconcile appearance invariance for understanding with sensitivity to detail for reconstruction. RAEs demonstrate reconstruction from continuous semantic features (Zheng et al., 2025), while LongCat-Next suggests that residual connections can carry low-level information across a semantic encoder (Meituan LongCat Team et al., 2026). This motivates us to directly leverage complementary cues by recombining multiple encoder depths, without even training the encoder itself. Meanwhile, quantization may collapse weakly expressed appearance differences into the same code. It therefore requires retaining the final semantic representation as an explicit anchor throughout quantization to preserve representation quality.

To tackle this, we introduce a Residual Modulator (ResMod) inspired by frozen semantic base with detail-aware modulation of PAE (Yue et al., 2026), which fuses intermediate features from the frozen encoder and learns a spatially varying correction to its final representation. Multi-level fusion exposes complementary spatial cues, and a zero-initialized residual update preserves the pretrained features at initialization. The resulting feature grid provides the quantizer with a shared representation whose semantic structure and local detail can be supervised by the two reconstruction branches.

Residual Modulator.

Figure 3(b) illustrates the module. Let {𝐇(ℓ)}ℓ=0L\{\mathbf{H}^{(\ell)}\}_{\ell=0}^{L} be the spatial tokens of the frozen vision transformer, with 𝐇(ℓ)∈ℝN×D\mathbf{H}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D}. We select early and deeper layers 𝒮⊆{0,…,L}\mathcal{S}\subseteq\{0,\ldots,L\} and fuse their normalized features:

𝐔=𝒯θ​(ℱθ​(Concatℓ∈𝒮⁡[LNℓ⁡(𝐇(ℓ))])),\mathbf{U}=\mathcal{T}_{\theta}\!\left(\mathcal{F}_{\theta}\!\left(\operatorname{Concat}_{\ell\in\mathcal{S}}\left[\operatorname{LN}_{\ell}(\mathbf{H}^{(\ell)})\right]\right)\right), (1)

where ℱθ\mathcal{F}_{\theta} projects the concatenated features to a common width and 𝒯θ\mathcal{T}_{\theta} is a lightweight stack of self-attention and feed-forward blocks. These intermediate taps provide direct access to spatial information at different levels of abstraction.

Let 𝐒=𝒜⁡(𝐇(L))\mathbf{S}=\mathcal{A}(\mathbf{H}^{(L)}) denote the semantic base on the quantizer grid, where 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the identity or the encoder’s spatial aggregation operator. We write NqN_{q} and CC for the number of spatial positions and the channel width on this grid, respectively. A projection 𝒫θ\mathcal{P}_{\theta} aligns 𝐔\mathbf{U} to this grid, and an affine head predicts token-wise scale and shift parameters:

(𝜸,𝜷)=Split⁡(𝒲θ​(LN⁡(𝒫θ​(𝐔)))),𝐙=𝐒+𝜸⊙𝐒+𝜷⏟𝚫θ.(\bm{\gamma},\bm{\beta})=\operatorname{Split}\!\left(\mathcal{W}_{\theta}\bigl(\operatorname{LN}(\mathcal{P}_{\theta}(\mathbf{U}))\bigr)\right),\qquad\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{S}+\underbrace{\bm{\gamma}\odot\mathbf{S}+\bm{\beta}}_{\bm{\Delta}_{\theta}}. (2)

The projection 𝒫θ\mathcal{P}_{\theta} also aggregates spatial tokens when 𝐒\mathbf{S} uses a coarser grid. We initialize 𝒲θ\mathcal{W}_{\theta} to zero, giving 𝚫θ=𝟎\bm{\Delta}_{\theta}=\mathbf{0} and 𝐙=𝐒\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{S} at initialization. Training then learns how to reweight the semantic base and add complementary information at each position. Thus, residual pathways within the encoder provide access to information across depth, and ResMod organizes this information for the discrete bottleneck while keeping the pretrained encoder fixed. As a result, ResMod only translates and rotates the pretrained features to enlarge representation capacity while preserving their original semantic structure.

2.4 Quantizer

The residual modulator enriches the features entering the discrete bottleneck, but retaining the exposed semantic distinctions and spatial detail requires sufficient quantization capacity at each spatial position. Motivated by evidence that multi-codebook quantization with a sufficient bit budget preserves semantic information at a level competitive with continuous representations (Zou et al., 2026a), we adopt grouped product quantization (Jégou et al., 2011) to expand this capacity while keeping the spatial token grid unchanged. As illustrated in Fig. 4, the features are factorized along the channel dimension and encoded using multiple codebooks, avoiding a prohibitively large monolithic vocabulary.

Let 𝐳t∈ℝC\mathbf{z}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{C} denote the feature presented to the quantizer at position tt of the modulated representation 𝐙∈ℝNq×C\mathbf{Z}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{q}\times C}. We partition its channels into GG disjoint groups, 𝐳t=Concatg=1G⁡[𝐳t(g)]\mathbf{z}_{t}=\operatorname{Concat}_{g=1}^{G}\left[\mathbf{z}_{t}^{(g)}\right], where each group has dimension d=C/Gd=C/G. Each group is assigned its own learned codebook ℰ(g)={𝐞k(g)}k=1K\mathcal{E}^{(g)}=\{\mathbf{e}_{k}^{(g)}\}_{k=1}^{K}, with 𝐞k(g)∈ℝd\mathbf{e}_{k}^{(g)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. Quantization selects the nearest entry within each group and concatenates the selected embeddings:

kt(g)=arg​mink∈{1,…,K}⁡‖𝐳t(g)−𝐞k(g)‖22,𝐤t=(kt(1),…,kt(G)),𝐜t=Concatg=1G[𝐞kt(g)(g)].\begin{gathered}k_{t}^{(g)}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}}\left\|\mathbf{z}_{t}^{(g)}-\mathbf{e}_{k}^{(g)}\right\|_{2}^{2},\\ \mathbf{k}_{t}=(k_{t}^{(1)},\ldots,k_{t}^{(G)}),\qquad\mathbf{c}_{t}=\operatorname{Concat}_{g=1}^{G}\left[\mathbf{e}_{k_{t}^{(g)}}^{(g)}\right].\end{gathered} (3)

Here 𝐤t\mathbf{k}_{t} is the discrete index tuple, whereas 𝐜t\mathbf{c}_{t} is its codebook embedding supplied to downstream decoders. Codebooks are shared across spatial positions, so the same quantization rule applies to variable-length grids at different image resolutions and aspect ratios. The resulting tuple belongs to the Cartesian product 𝒦={1,…,K}G\mathcal{K}=\{1,\ldots,K\}^{G}, giving a combinatorial code space with

|𝒦|=KG,Bposition=G​log2​K,Bimage=Nq​G​log2​K,|\mathcal{K}|=K^{G},\qquad B_{\mathrm{position}}=G\log_{2}K,\qquad B_{\mathrm{image}}=N_{q}G\log_{2}K, (4)

where NqN_{q} denotes the number of spatial positions on the quantizer grid. With GG codebooks of KK entries each, the quantizer admits up to KGK^{G} combinations without explicitly storing a vocabulary of that size. At fixed KK, increasing GG raises the nominal bit budget while leaving NqN_{q} unchanged, but introduces more code indices to model. This budget characterizes the available discrete alphabet, not the empirical entropy or semantic information retained; greater capacity alone does not guarantee faithful reconstruction. Separate codebook lookups also do not imply statistically independent indices, as the groups encode the same visual content.

The quantization groups operate on the fused representation without predefined semantic or perceptual roles. Stacking the embeddings in spatial order gives 𝐂=[𝐜1,…,𝐜Nq]⊤∈ℝNq×C\mathbf{C}=[\mathbf{c}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{c}_{N_{q}}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{q}\times C}. The resulting matrix serves as a shared input to the semantic and pixel decoders, whose complementary objectives encourage the codes to retain both pretrained semantic structure and reconstruction-relevant detail. Residual modulation thus determines which information enters the bottleneck, grouped quantization supplies the capacity to encode it, and dual-decoder supervision guides how that capacity is used.

2.5 Dual-Branch Reconstruction

A general-purpose visual vocabulary must preserve pretrained semantic structure while retaining the fine-grained visual detail needed to recover the original visual signal. These requirements concern different output spaces but must be satisfied by the same discrete codes. We therefore introduce two specialized decoders that share the quantized representation. The semantic branch aligns the codes with continuous visual features, while the pixel branch supervises image reconstruction.

Representation Reconstruction Branch.

We take the quantized feature matrix 𝐂\mathbf{C}, as defined in Section 2.4, as the input to both decoders. The semantic decoder 𝒟sem\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{sem}} maps the quantized embeddings back to the continuous feature space after residual modulation,

𝐙^=𝒟sem​(𝐂).\widehat{\mathbf{Z}}=\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{sem}}(\mathbf{C}). (5)

We supervise this prediction with a fixed post-ResMod target 𝐙⋆\mathbf{Z}^{\star}, combining feature regression with cosine alignment,

ℒsem=1−cos⁡(𝐙^,sg⁡(𝐙⋆))+λMSEsem​‖𝐙^−sg⁡(𝐙⋆)‖22,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sem}}=1-\cos\!\left(\widehat{\mathbf{Z}},\operatorname{sg}(\mathbf{Z}^{\star})\right)+\lambda_{\mathrm{MSE}}^{\mathrm{sem}}\left\|\widehat{\mathbf{Z}}-\operatorname{sg}(\mathbf{Z}^{\star})\right\|_{2}^{2}, (6)

where sg⁡(⋅)\operatorname{sg}(\cdot) stops gradients through the target path. The target is produced by a frozen ResMod, as specified in Section 3.1. We find that cosine loss alone can be small even for inaccurate reconstructions when a dominant shared feature mean concentrates features in a narrow cone, consistent with representation anisotropy (Ethayarajh, 2019). The MSE term complements directional alignment by constraining absolute feature values. Reconstructing this representation encourages the codes to retain the semantic structure inherited from the pretrained backbone together with the information introduced by residual modulation.

Pixel Reconstruction Branch.

Feature alignment alone does not directly constrain fidelity to the original image. We therefore decode the same embeddings into pixels, first restoring and expanding their spatial grid through token unmerging,

𝐱^=𝒟pix​(𝒰⁡(𝐂,hq,wq)),\widehat{\mathbf{x}}=\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pix}}\bigl(\mathcal{U}(\mathbf{C};h_{q},w_{q})\bigr), (7)

where (hq,wq)(h_{q},w_{q}) is the quantized grid size, 𝒰\mathcal{U} denotes token unmerging and spatial expansion, and 𝒟pix\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pix}} is the pixel decoder. We train this branch with five complementary reconstruction losses,

ℒpix=λ1​ℒ1+λMSEpix​ℒMSE+λLPIPS​ℒLPIPS+λperc​ℒperc+λGram​ℒGram.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pix}}=\lambda_{1}\mathcal{L}_{1}+\lambda_{\mathrm{MSE}}^{\mathrm{pix}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MSE}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{LPIPS}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LPIPS}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{perc}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{perc}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{Gram}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Gram}}. (8)

The λ\lambda coefficients balance the five objectives; the pixel MSE weight λMSEpix\lambda_{\mathrm{MSE}}^{\mathrm{pix}} is distinct from the feature MSE weight λMSEsem\lambda_{\mathrm{MSE}}^{\mathrm{sem}}. All terms compare the reconstruction 𝐱^\widehat{\mathbf{x}} with the input 𝐱\mathbf{x}. Here ℒ1\mathcal{L}_{1} and ℒMSE\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MSE}} denote mean absolute and mean squared pixel errors, respectively. ℒLPIPS\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LPIPS}} uses VGG features to measure perceptual similarity across multiple layers. The ConvNeXt-S-based perceptual loss ℒperc\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{perc}} applies MSE to the network outputs to align high-level recognition responses. ℒGram\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Gram}} matches Gram matrices of VGG features to preserve texture and channel correlations. The two branches jointly constrain the information retained by the shared vocabulary through

ℒdual=λsem​ℒsem+λpix​ℒpix.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dual}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{sem}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sem}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{pix}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pix}}. (9)

The semantic objective anchors reconstruction in the modulated feature space, while the pixel objective requires access to texture, color, and spatial detail. Section 3.1 describes how these objectives are introduced progressively to train the shared bottleneck and residual pathway.

Flexible Encoding and Decoding at Arbitrary Resolutions.

We retain each image’s token-grid dimensions throughout encoding and decoding. The encoder maps an input image to an hq×wqh_{q}\times w_{q} feature grid, which quantization converts into codebook embeddings without altering its spatial layout. For semantic reconstruction, the semantic decoder recovers a continuous feature at each grid position. For image reconstruction, 𝒰⁡(𝐂,hq,wq)\mathcal{U}(\mathbf{C};h_{q},w_{q}) uses the recorded dimensions to arrange and spatially expand the quantized tokens before the pixel decoder reconstructs an RGB image at the input resolution. Both branches therefore remain spatially aligned with the input image across varying grid dimensions and aspect ratios.

2.6 Refiner

Although the ViT pixel decoder preserves image content faithfully, standard practices often employ a refiner module to further enhance its visual perceptual quality. We introduce a code-conditioned Refiner for high-fidelity decoding with sharper, more realistic details (Fig. 6). Unlike conventional super-resolution models conditioned on decoded RGB images, our Refiner directly conditions on discrete visual codes, avoiding information loss introduced by intermediate pixel decoding. It also requires no text conditioning, whose semantic priors may alter source content and constrain image editing. Built on a pretrained image-generation prior, the Refiner replaces the ViT pixel decoder with a flow decoder using discrete codes as its sole conditioning input. We train a multi-step teacher and distill it into an efficient one-step student.

Code-conditioned refinement.

Given an encoder observation 𝐱L\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{L}} and a target image 𝐱H\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{H}}, the frozen tokenizer maps 𝐱L\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{L}} to codebook embeddings 𝐂\mathbf{C}. These embeddings condition a pretrained generative transformer through two paths: a context adapter supplies tokens to its joint-attention stream, and a time-conditioned spatial adapter injects aligned residuals into the latent input and selected transformer layers. Let 𝐇ref(j)\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{ref}}^{(j)} denote the token-feature matrix at layer jj of the Refiner and τ\tau denote flow time. The layer update is

𝐇ref(j+1)=ℬ(j)​(𝐇ref(j),𝒞ϕ​(𝐂))+𝒥ϕ(j)​(𝒜ϕ​(𝐂,τ)),\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{ref}}^{(j+1)}=\mathcal{B}^{(j)}\!\left(\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{ref}}^{(j)},\mathcal{C}_{\phi}(\mathbf{C})\right)+\mathcal{J}_{\phi}^{(j)}\!\left(\mathcal{A}_{\phi}(\mathbf{C},\tau)\right), (10)

where 𝒞ϕ\mathcal{C}_{\phi} forms global context tokens and 𝒥ϕ(j)∘𝒜ϕ\mathcal{J}_{\phi}^{(j)}\circ\mathcal{A}_{\phi} provides spatially aligned residual features. The injection projections are zero-initialized, so the added spatial path initially preserves the backbone computation. The global path carries scene-level context, while the spatial path aligns generated features with corresponding code locations. Because both adapters operate on code token grids, the Refiner supports variable resolutions and aspect ratios. The teacher is trained by flow matching in the latent space of a frozen image autoencoder. Let 𝐲0=𝒱⁡(𝐱H)\mathbf{y}_{0}=\mathcal{V}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{H}}), and use the noise level τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1] as the flow coordinate, with 𝐲τ=(1−τ)​𝐲0+τ​ϵ\mathbf{y}_{\tau}=(1-\tau)\mathbf{y}_{0}+\tau\bm{\epsilon} and ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈)\bm{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}). We optimize

ℒFM=𝔼⁡[w⁡(τ)​‖𝐯θ​(𝐲τ,τ,𝐂)−(ϵ−𝐲0)‖22].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[w(\tau)\left\|\mathbf{v}_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}_{\tau},\tau,\mathbf{C})-(\bm{\epsilon}-\mathbf{y}_{0})\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]. (11)

Here 𝐯θ\mathbf{v}_{\theta} is the conditional velocity field and w⁡(τ)w(\tau) is the timestep-dependent loss weight.

One-step adversarial distillation.

The one-step student is initialized from the frozen teacher and retains the same code condition. Training combines latent-space regression to the teacher’s multi-step output with a stop-gradient correction derived from the teacher’s noise predictions on identically perturbed student and teacher outputs. Adversarial supervision comes from a time-aware discriminator on features extracted by the frozen teacher, using ground-truth image latents as real samples and a hinge discriminator loss.

3 Implementation

3.1 Training Stage

Our optimization strategy separates learning complementary visual detail from adapting the enriched representation to a discrete bottleneck. As illustrated in Fig. 7, training proceeds through continuous pixel pretraining, discrete semantic reconstruction, and joint reconstruction. The tokenizer combines a pretrained Qwen3-VL ViT (∼\sim400M), frozen throughout training to preserve its semantic representations, with a residual modulator (∼\sim100M), totaling ∼\sim500M parameters. We denote by ℰ⁡(𝐱)\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{x}) the collection of intermediate and final ViT features supplied to ResMod ℛ\mathcal{R}, and by 𝒬\mathcal{Q} the grouped quantizer.

Stage 1: Continuous Pixel Pretraining.

We first train ResMod to recover the original visual signal from the representation encoder. ResMod produces 𝐙=ℛ⁡(ℰ⁡(𝐱))\mathbf{Z}=\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{x})), which is passed to the pixel reconstruction branch. Minimizing ℒpix\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pix}} jointly trains ResMod and the pixel decoder while the ViT remains frozen. This stage initializes the residual pathway to expose reconstruction-relevant information before a discrete vocabulary is introduced.

Stage 2: Discrete Semantic Reconstruction.

This stage initializes discrete representations that preserve semantic structure while retaining the pixel detail introduced by ResMod in Stage 1. We freeze both the ViT and ResMod, using the ResMod output 𝐙\mathbf{Z} as the quantizer input and the fixed semantic reconstruction target 𝐙⋆\mathbf{Z}^{\star}. The quantizer and semantic decoder are jointly trained with ℒsem\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sem}} to reconstruct this detail-enriched representation from 𝐂=𝒬⁡(𝐙)\mathbf{C}=\mathcal{Q}(\mathbf{Z}). In parallel, the pixel decoder is trained with ℒpix\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pix}} on detached codes sg⁡(𝐂)\operatorname{sg}(\mathbf{C}), establishing an initial mapping from discrete codes to pixels. Stopping gradients at this interface prevents the pixel objective from disrupting semantic learning while the discrete representations are being initialized.

Stage 3: Joint Reconstruction.

This stage jointly refines the discrete representations for semantic and pixel reconstruction. We unfreeze the encoding ResMod while retaining a frozen teacher copy to prevent target drift during joint optimization. With student ℛS\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{S}} and teacher ℛT\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{T}}, the semantic target 𝐙⋆\mathbf{Z}^{\star} now comes from the frozen teacher, while the quantized features 𝐂\mathbf{C} come from the trainable student:

𝐙⋆\displaystyle\mathbf{Z}^{\star} =ℛT​(ℰ​(𝐱)),\displaystyle=\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{T}}\bigl(\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{x})\bigr), (12)
𝐂\displaystyle\mathbf{C} =𝒬⁡(ℛS​(ℰ⁡(𝐱))).\displaystyle=\mathcal{Q}\!\left(\mathcal{R}^{\mathrm{S}}\bigl(\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{x})\bigr)\right).

The quantizer and both decoders continue training from Stage 2 under ℒdual\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dual}}. The semantic branch reconstructs the fixed target 𝐙⋆\mathbf{Z}^{\star}, while the pixel branch is no longer detached, allowing pixel gradients to update the quantizer and student ResMod. The ViT and teacher ResMod remain frozen throughout.

3.2 Training Data

The tokenization and de-tokenization training corpus combines diverse image sources to support semantic representation learning and maintain fine-grained pixel information. These sources are grouped into three complementary categories according to visual content. Tokenizer training uses images exclusively for dual-branch supervision, with a carefully controlled resolution distribution to support arbitrary-resolution training.

General-Domain Images.

LAION (Schuhmann et al., 2022), COYO (Byeon et al., 2022), and DataComp (Gadre et al., 2023), together with images from Recap-DataComp-1B (Li et al., 2024) and CapsFusion (Yu et al., 2024b), provide broad coverage of objects, scenes, and visual styles. An in-house image corpus further expands the diversity of the training data.

Text-Rich Images and Documents.

Selected subsets of TextAtlas5M (Wang et al., 2025a) include book covers, images containing long words, academic papers, and presentation slides. Chinese- and English-language book and news pages, along with additional OCR-oriented collections, extend coverage to dense text, small characters, and complex document layouts. Infographic collections and ChartGalaxy (Li et al., 2025) further contribute information-dense content, including charts and tables, where spatial relationships among visual elements are critical to interpretation.

Fine-Grained and High-aesthetic Images.

Face-focused LAION subsets, images derived from SA-1B (Kirillov et al., 2023), and an in-house collection of high-aesthetic-quality images enrich the corpus with detailed facial structures, local textures, and varied image compositions.

Training begins at a fixed resolution of 256×256256\times 256 using a limited set of image sources to facilitate rapid convergence, then progressively transitions to native-resolution training at resolutions up to 2K on a broader data mixture. During this transition, sampling maintains a balanced distribution across resolution ranges. Images are resized to approximately preserve their aspect ratios, align spatial dimensions with the encoder stride, and keep sequence lengths within the token budget. Across all stages, the model is trained on several hundred billion tokens.

4 Experiment

We evaluate dNaViT across five complementary tasks to assess the generality of its shared discrete representation. Image reconstruction measures the preservation of fine-grained detail, while frozen-feature classification and multimodal understanding assess semantic discriminability, transfer robustness, and visual reasoning. Autoregressive text-to-image generation and instruction-guided editing further examine the utility of the learned codes for conditional synthesis and image manipulation.

4.1 Image Reconstruction

Evaluation Setup.

We evaluate reconstruction on ImageNet-1K (Russakovsky et al., 2015) and TokBench (Wu et al., 2025c) to assess whether dNaViT’s shared discrete vocabulary preserves overall image fidelity and fine-grained textual and facial detail. We denote the dNaViT variants with 16 and 64 quantization groups as dNaViT-G16 and dNaViT-G64, respectively; both use a vision transformer (ViT) pixel decoder without refinement and a spatial downsampling factor of f=32f=32. dNaViT-G16-R denotes the 16-group variant with the ViT pixel decoder replaced by the code-conditioned flow decoder (Refiner; Sec. 2.6). On ImageNet-1K, we report PSNR and SSIM at 256×256256\times 256, 512×512512\times 512, and 1024×10241024\times 1024, using the full validation set and standard preprocessing. On TokBench, we report text recognition accuracy (T-ACC), normalized edit similarity (T-NED), and face similarity (F-Sim) at 512×512512\times 512 and 1024×10241024\times 1024, with equal weighting across the official instance-scale buckets. Baseline scores are taken from published reports. Differences in evaluation protocols and training configurations preclude controlled or rate-matched comparisons.

ImageNet Reconstruction.

As shown in Table 1, dNaViT-G64 achieves 25.41 dB PSNR with 0.76 SSIM at 256×256256\times 256 and 28.12 dB PSNR with 0.81 SSIM at 512×512512\times 512. At 1024×10241024\times 1024, it reaches 32.90 dB PSNR and 0.91 SSIM, compared with 28.93 dB and 0.81 for dNaViT-G16. These results indicate that dNaViT retains substantial reconstruction-relevant information within its shared discrete representation across all three resolutions.

Fine-Grained Reconstruction on TokBench.

Table 2 shows that dNaViT-G64 achieves results comparable to those reported for LlamaGen-f​8f8 and higher scores than DC-AE-f​32f32 on all three metrics at both resolutions. At 1024×10241024\times 1024, it attains 63.08% T-ACC, 78.27% T-NED, and 0.67 F-Sim. The scale-stratified results in Table 3 further show consistent gains over dNaViT-G16 across all instance sizes. However, dNaViT-G16 and dNaViT-G64 differ in training configuration and duration, so this comparison does not isolate the effect of quantization group count. These findings indicate that dNaViT preserves textual and facial detail beyond global image structure. Small text nevertheless remains challenging, and a performance gap persists relative to stronger reconstruction models such as FLUX.1.

4.2 Image Classification

Evaluation Setup.

We evaluate frozen representations through linear probing on ImageNet-1K (Deng et al., 2009; Russakovsky et al., 2015) and direct transfer to ImageNet-A (Hendrycks et al., 2021b), ImageNet-R (Hendrycks et al., 2021a), ImageNet-V2 (Recht et al., 2019), ImageNet-Sketch (Wang et al., 2019), and ObjectNet (Barbu et al., 2019). All representations have a 16×1616\times 16 spatial grid before FP32 mean pooling, followed by non-affine synchronized batch normalization and a linear classifier. Each encoder retains its original input resolution and normalization. Classifiers are trained exclusively on ImageNet-1K for 10 epochs using cross-entropy and SGD with momentum 0.9, Nesterov acceleration, zero weight decay, a global batch size of 1024, and a peak learning rate of 0.1. ImageNet-A and ImageNet-R use their respective 200-class subsets. ObjectNet evaluation covers 18,574 images from the official 113 overlapping categories, with many-to-one label mapping and red-border removal.

Results.

As shown in Table 5, continuous dNaViT closely matches QwenViT on ImageNet-1K and all five distribution-shift benchmarks. Discrete dNaViT achieves 79.47% on ImageNet-1K, 0.93 percentage points below its continuous counterpart. Among the evaluated discrete representations, it achieves the highest accuracy on ImageNet-1K, ImageNet-A, and ImageNet-V2, reaching 56.35% and 69.81% on the latter two. Its transfer performance is not uniformly lower than that of continuous dNaViT: it attains 68.09% on ImageNet-R and 59.79% on ObjectNet, compared with 65.19% and 56.48%, respectively. UniTok remains stronger on ImageNet-R, ImageNet-Sketch, and ObjectNet. These results suggest that dNaViT’s discrete representation preserves substantial linearly accessible semantic information, although its relative transfer performance depends on the target distribution.

4.3 Visual Understanding

We evaluate whether the discrete codes learned with both semantic and pixel reconstruction retain the information needed for multimodal understanding. We report general and mathematical reasoning separately from text, document, and chart understanding.

Training Setup.

We pair the frozen visual tokenizer dNaViT-G16 with Qwen3-8B and train through alignment, pre-training, mid-training, and supervised fine-tuning using approximately 70B, 150B, 60B, and 30B tokens, respectively. Alignment uses image–text pairs, while pre-training covers image captioning, interleaved image–text sequences, OCR, grounding, multi-image data, and text-only data. Mid-training focuses on STEM and OCR, supplemented with general image–text and text-only data. Supervised fine-tuning uses visual instruction-following data covering general understanding, STEM, OCR, and document tasks.

Evaluation Setup.

For general understanding, we use MMMU (Yue et al., 2024), MMMU-Pro (Yue et al., 2025a), RealWorldQA (xAI, 2024), and MMStar (Chen et al., 2024b); for mathematical reasoning, we use MathVista (Lu et al., 2024) and MathVision. For fine-grained visual understanding, we evaluate OCRBench (Liu et al., 2024), OCRBench V2 (Fu et al., 2026), DocVQA (Mathew et al., 2021), InfoVQA (Mathew et al., 2022), ChartQA (Masry et al., 2022), CharXiv (Wang et al., 2024c), and OmniDocBench (Ouyang et al., 2025). The comparison includes models that use continuous visual representations and models that pass visual information through a discrete bottleneck before language-model processing. These are model-level comparisons with potentially different training data, image resolutions, prompting, and scoring protocols.

STEM and General Understanding.

Table 4 demonstrates strong STEM reasoning and general understanding with discrete visual tokens. dNaViT leads the discrete models in this comparison and remains competitive with strong continuous-representation models, including comparable performance to Qwen3-VL-8B on MathVista. These results demonstrate that discrete visual representations can support strong multimodal reasoning and general understanding.

OCR, Document, and Chart Understanding.

Discrete representations are often assumed to discard the fine-grained visual details required for OCR and document understanding (Yu et al., 2026). Table 6 shows that dNaViT outperforms the compared discrete models and substantially narrows the gap to strong continuous models on text-centric tasks. It performs comparably to Qwen3-VL-8B on DocVQA and OmniDocBench and leads the compared models on both CharXiv tasks. These results demonstrate that discrete visual representations can support fine-grained OCR, document understanding, and chart interpretation, challenging the view that they are inherently unsuitable for fine-grained visual tasks.

4.4 Visual Generation and Editing

Evaluation Setup.

We evaluate text-to-image generation of dNaViT-G16-R on GenEval2, Qwen-Image-Bench (Li et al., 2026), SpatialGenEval, and LongText-Bench (Geng et al., 2025). These benchmarks assess compositional alignment, prompt following, spatial reasoning, and text rendering in English and Chinese. For instruction-guided image editing, we use the English full set of GEdit-Bench (Liu et al., 2025) and report semantic consistency (SC), perceptual quality (PQ), and the benchmark’s overall score.

Text-to-Image Generation.

Table 7 compares proprietary, diffusion, and autoregressive models on compositional generation, spatial reasoning, and text rendering, using the benchmark settings summarized in its caption. dNaViT-8B attains the highest GenEval2 GM (49.5) among the models that report this metric and the second-highest SpatialGenEval score (0.68), behind SenseNova-U1-8B (0.72). Its QwenImageBench score of 52.17 exceeds every open-weight baseline while remaining below the proprietary systems (54.07–64.69), and it reaches 0.94 and 0.94 on the English and Chinese subsets of LongText-Bench, within the range of the open-weight models and below the strongest proprietary systems on Chinese text. Baseline values are reported results and may use different training data, sampling configurations, and evaluation protocols.

Instruction-Guided Image Editing.

Table 8 compares image editing with proprietary and open models. SC measures consistency with the editing instruction and PQ measures perceptual quality. We retain the benchmark-reported overall scores rather than recomputing them as the arithmetic mean of SC and PQ.

5 Analysis

5.1 Effectiveness of ResMod

We compare ResMod (a zero-initialized residual modulation module with the pretrained encoder frozen) with SelfDistill (a shallow fusion baseline that trains the encoder while matching its final-layer features to a frozen teacher) Tang et al. (2025b); Yue et al. (2025b). As shown in Fig. 8, ResMod maintains lower pixel MSE and representation cosine losses during the late training stage. The zoomed 10k–11k interval shows that both advantages remain stable rather than arising from isolated fluctuations. These results indicate that ResMod preserves high-level semantic representations while retaining more fine-grained visual details, resulting in more effective fusion of pixel and semantic information.

We further assess the effectiveness of ResMod on visual understanding tasks. These experiments use Qwen3-1.7B as the language backbone, with the visual tokenizer kept frozen. In Table 9, settings 1 and 3 train understanding models on frozen continuous features without and with pretrained ResMod, respectively. For the training-free setting 2, we directly insert pretrained ResMod into the trained model from 1 at evaluation time, without any further parameter updates. Setting 2 maintains comparable average performance to 1, even without retraining the LLM. Together with the reconstruction results above, this provides further evidence that ResMod can enrich pixel-level information while preserving pretrained semantic information.

5.2 Comparison between Discrete and Continuous Approaches

Using the same understanding training and evaluation setup as in Sec. 5.1, we compare discrete and continuous visual representations. Table 9 shows comparable performance across general understanding, OCR, and document benchmarks. This observation is consistent with the scaling analysis in LongCat-Next (Meituan LongCat Team et al., 2026), which finds that discrete visual embeddings require more training data because they are learned from scratch, and that increasing the data scale progressively closes the gap with continuous models. Together, these findings suggest that discrete visual representations can match continuous features in multimodal understanding.

5.3 Comparison of Pixel Reconstruction

Fig. 9 isolates the effect of the decoding strategy while keeping the visual representation and input resolution fixed. The ViT pixel decoder maps the discrete code embeddings directly to pixel values. This path reliably preserves the global layout, color distribution, and semantic content, but tends to over-smooth high-frequency information. Consequently, small text, fine boundaries, and repetitive textures often appear blurred or partially merged.

The flow-based Refiner, used in dNaViT-G16-R, conditions the decoder on the same discrete representations while leveraging a pretrained generative prior. Rather than relying solely on direct pixel regression, it recovers sharper letter contours, finer textures, and more convincing high-frequency details. These improvements are obtained without changing the underlying codes, and the generated results remain consistent with the structure and semantic content specified by the tokenizer.

The advantage becomes particularly evident under high spatial compression. Even with a compact token representation, the Refiner continues to recover legible text and boundary details that the pixel decoder leaves ambiguous. This indicates that the discrete representation retains substantial information beyond what is recovered by direct pixel decoding, and that a generative decoder can realize this information more effectively. The comparison therefore separates the capacity of the learned tokenizer from the limitations of the decoding head, highlighting the benefit of our code-conditioned refinement under highly compressed representations.

5.4 Qualitative Visual Understanding Examples

We present qualitative examples of our 8B understanding model on challenging visual inputs: dense full-page documents in English (Fig. 10) and Chinese (Fig. 11), cursive handwriting (Fig. 13), an engineering drawing (Fig. 13), and diagram-grounded reasoning (Figs. 15 and 15). Each example places the source image inside the model response, with the instruction and the response set. Responses are reproduced verbatim, including the model’s own errors. Long transcriptions are truncated at a paragraph boundary and marked as continuing, and for examples in which the model produces an explicit reasoning trace, only the final response is shown. These examples illustrate fine-grained recognition and reasoning rather than replace quantitative evaluation.

6 Conclusion

This work presents dNaViT, a foundational visual component acting as a native-resolution tokenizer that turns discrete codes into universal visual primitives. Through lightweight residual modulation, grouped product quantization, and progressive dual-branch optimization, dNaViT successfully reconciles high-level semantic abstraction with fine-grained visual reconstruction. Further code-conditioned refinement enhances perceptual fidelity without altering the unified representation. Across understanding, generation, and editing tasks, dNaViT matches or exceeds task-specific baselines under a significantly smaller data budget. These findings demonstrate that a shared discrete token space can serve as a universal visual currency, paving the way for fully unified, native multimodal intelligence.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
